discrete-vram.rule: The card's VRAM, less the driver and desktop share. fit.mjs owns that reserve (0.5 GB + 5% of VRAM).
notes: The card driving the display holds 0.3–1.5 GB on Windows (compositor, browser surfaces); a CUDA, ROCm or Vulkan context takes 0.3–0.5 GB.
On Windows the NVIDIA driver spills over-full VRAM into shared system memory instead of failing, so an oversized model 'loads' and then crawls.

apple-metal.rule: Metal's default recommendedMaxWorkingSetSize: 2/3 of RAM when RAM ≤ 32 GB, 3/4 when RAM ≥ 36 GB.

raise.headroom_rule: leave max(4 GB, 12% of RAM) for macOS
raise.note: Resets at restart. Setting it to 0 restores the default. Leave room for macOS: going too high causes heavy swapping or a kernel panic.

notes: Every logged datapoint on macOS 13–15 follows the rule exactly (classic column). macOS 26 (Tahoe) logs show larger shares; we can't detect the macOS version reliably (Safari's user agent is frozen), so the classic rule is the default and is conservative on macOS 26.
The decompiled rule (reserve 33.3%, or 25% above 32 GiB) is reverse-engineered, not documented.

amd-apu.applies_to: AMD laptop/mini-PC/handheld APUs with 128-bit memory (780M, 890M, Z1, Z2…)
amd-apu.rule: Linux/SteamOS: the GTT limit, 50% of RAM (plus the BIOS carve-out). Windows: 50% of RAM shared, or the device's 'GPU memory' setting if it is known and larger.

raise.windows: Raise the GPU memory in the BIOS (UMA Frame Buffer Size), AMD Software (Variable Graphics Memory), or the handheld's own app (Armoury Crate, Legion Space).
raise.linux: Add the kernel option ttm.pages_limit=<4 KiB pages> (amdgpu.gttsize is deprecated).

notes: What matters more on these chips is bandwidth: past the GPU share, the processor runs the remaining layers from the same memory at a similar speed, so a small share costs little.

amd-halo.applies_to: Strix Halo / Gorgon Halo (Ryzen AI Max), 256-bit unified memory
amd-halo.rule: Default 50% of RAM (Windows shared memory, Linux GTT). Raised: Windows Variable Graphics Memory up to 96 GB on 128 GB (75%); Linux ttm.pages_limit up to RAM − 8 GB.

raise.windows: AMD Software (Adrenalin) > Performance > Tuning > Variable Graphics Memory: choose the largest size (96 GB on a 128 GB machine).
raise.linux: Add ttm.pages_limit=31457280 (120 GiB in 4 KiB pages; scale to your RAM) to the kernel command line and reboot.

steam-deck.rule: 6 GB: what llama.cpp's Vulkan backend reported as usable on a Deck (6101 MiB).
notes: The UMA setting (1 GB default, 4 GB option) is not the limit on SteamOS: the GPU also borrows main memory through GTT. A model larger than 6 GB still runs, with the processor taking the remaining layers.

intel-igpu.applies_to: Intel Arc integrated graphics (Meteor Lake, Lunar Lake, Arrow Lake, Panther Lake)
intel-igpu.rule: 50% of RAM (Windows shared GPU memory; Linux i915/xe similar).

raise.windows: Intel Graphics Software has a 'Shared GPU Memory Override' on Core Ultra with Arc graphics (supported CPUs and the maximum are unverified).

flags: The Windows 50% rule is widely documented but no Microsoft primary source was found.

nvidia-unified-linux.rule: All of RAM less the OS reserve: CUDA allocates from the whole pool on these Linux systems.

flags: Unverified for RTX Spark: NVIDIA hasn't said how much memory Windows gives the GPU.

cpu-only.rule: No fast pool. The model runs from system RAM (RAM less the OS reserve, which fit.mjs owns).

presets.label: Office desktop, no graphics card, 16 GB

steps.text: Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. If it opens as a small window, click "More details".
Click Performance (the line-graph icon on the left in Windows 11, a tab along the top in Windows 10).
Click GPU 0, and GPU 1 if there is one. The graphics chip's name is at the top right. Under the graphs, "Dedicated GPU memory" is the graphics card's own memory (its VRAM).
steps.caption: Task Manager's Performance page with "GPU 1, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Laptop GPU" selected. The left column lists CPU, Memory, Disk, Wi-Fi, GPU 0 and GPU 1. At the bottom: "Dedicated GPU memory 0.4/8.0 GB" and "Shared GPU memory 0.1/15.9 GB".

steps.text: Two GPUs? On most laptops one is built in (Intel UHD/Iris/Arc or "AMD Radeon Graphics", with a tiny dedicated memory) and one is the real graphics card (NVIDIA GeForce or AMD Radeon RX, with 4 GB or more). Pick the real card.

Click Memory. The total is at the top right (for example "32.0 GB"). Below the graph, "Speed" (for example 5600 MT/s) and "Slots used" (for example "2 of 2") tell us how fast it is. "1 of 2" means one stick, which is half as fast.
steps.caption: Task Manager's Memory page: "32.0 GB" top right, and below the graph "Speed: 5600 MT/s", "Slots used: 2 of 2", "Form factor: SODIMM".

steps.text: Another way: Start > Settings > System > About shows Processor and Installed RAM.
steps.caption: Settings > About: a "Device specifications" card listing Device name, Processor, Installed RAM ("16.0 GB (15.7 GB usable)") and System type.

steps.text: Click the Apple menu () at the top left, then About This Mac.
steps.caption: The About This Mac window: a picture of the Mac, its name in bold ("MacBook Pro, 14-inch, 2023"), then Chip "Apple M3 Pro", Memory "18 GB", Serial number and macOS version.

steps.text: "Chip" tells you the chip (for example Apple M2) and "Memory" the amount (for example 16 GB). That memory is shared by everything, including AI, so it's the number that matters.
If it says "Processor" (Intel) instead of "Chip", your Mac is an older Intel Mac. Local AI runs on it only slowly, on the processor.
For the number of graphics cores: Apple menu > System Settings > General > About > System Report > Graphics/Displays, "Total Number of Cores". Most people don't need this.
GNOME (Ubuntu, Fedora): open Settings > System > About. It lists Memory, Processor and Graphics.
KDE (Kubuntu, Fedora KDE, Bazzite): open Info Center (or System Settings > About this System).

Or paste these into a terminal (they only read, never change anything): `lspci | grep -iE 'vga|3d'` lists graphics chips; `nvidia-smi` shows an NVIDIA card and its memory; `free -h` shows memory (the "total" on the Mem: row).
Both Steam Deck models have 16 GB of memory, so for AI they are nearly the same. The OLED is about 16% faster.
The quick check: if your Deck's display settings go up to 90 Hz, it's an OLED. The LCD model stops at 60 Hz.
Other clues: the OLED has a bigger 7.4" screen with thinner borders. In Desktop Mode, Info Center shows the processor as "AMD Custom APU 0405" (LCD) or "AMD Custom APU 0932" (OLED).
Not sure? Pick Steam Deck LCD: it's the cautious choice, and the results are almost the same.
ROG Ally or Ally X? On Windows, Settings > System > About shows the model (RC71L is the Ally, RC72LA the Ally X) and the memory (16 GB or 24 GB).
Legion Go or Go S? If the controllers slide off the sides, it's a Legion Go (or Go 2); if they don't, it's a Go S.

chromeos.title: Chromebook

steps.text: Open the Diagnostics app (search the launcher for "Diagnostics"). It shows the processor and the memory.
Most Chromebooks have no graphics card and 4–8 GB of memory, which suits only small models, and running them needs Linux (Settings > Advanced > Developers > Linux development environment).
